title: Surface Areas and Volumes: Combined Solids
seo_title: Surface Areas and Volumes Class 10 Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Chapter 12)
standard_code: Class 10, Chapter 12: Surface Areas and Volumes
standard_text: Surface areas and volumes of combinations of any two of the following: cubes, cuboids, spheres, hemispheres and right circular cylinders/cones (summary of the CBSE syllabus)
meta_desc: Class 10 Surface Areas and Volumes worksheet (NCERT Chapter 12): formulae, surface area and volume of combined solids, solids with parts removed, problems in litres and rupees. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Combined solid: add only the visible surfaces
key_sub: Volumes simply add up (or subtract what is removed).
body_html:
How it works

Cylinder: CSA 2πrh, V πr²h. Cone: CSA πrl (l = √(r² + h²)), V ⅓πr²h. Sphere: S 4πr², V 4/3 πr³. Hemisphere: CSA 2πr², TSA 3πr², V ⅔πr³.

Surface area of a combination: add only the surfaces you can see. The faces where the solids are joined are hidden.

Volume of a combination: add the volumes (or subtract the part that is removed).

Example

A toy is a cone (r = 3.5 cm, h = 12 cm) on a hemisphere. Find its surface area.

l = √(3.5² + 12²) = 12.5

πrl + 2πr² = 137.5 + 77

Answer: 214.5 cm²

Example

A cylinder (r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm) has a cone (h = 6 cm) on top. Find its volume.

πr²h = 1,540

⅓πr²h = 308

Answer: 1,848 cm³

Common mistakes

  • Adding the total surface areas of both solids. The joined circles are not on the outside.
  • Using the slant height l in the volume of a cone. Volume uses the vertical height h.
  • Using 1 m³ = 100 litres. 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.

faq.q: How do I find the surface area of a combination of solids?
faq.a: Add the curved or flat surfaces that are visible. Do not include the faces where the two solids are joined.

faq.q: How do I find the volume of a combination of solids?
faq.a: Add the volumes of the parts. If a part is removed, subtract its volume.

faq.q: What is the total surface area of a solid hemisphere?
faq.a: 3πr²: the curved surface 2πr² plus the flat circle πr².
NCERT problems often use radii that are multiples of 7, so 22/7 gives exact answers. Use 3.14 when the question says so.
